subject: Computer Networking
title: Spine-Leaf Architecture
description: A quick win: understand Spine-Leaf Architecture.

hook.text: Data centers ditched the traditional tree. They use a flat, fast design called spine-leaf.

buildup.text: Leaf switches connect to servers. Spine switches connect to every leaf. Any two servers are two hops apart.

discovery.text: Consistent hop count means predictable latency. Any server pair communicates in the same time.

twist.text: Adding capacity is easy: add more spines. The architecture scales horizontally without a full redesign.

climax.text: ECMP spreads traffic across all spines evenly. No single spine becomes a bottleneck.

punchline.text: Spine-leaf: flat, fast, and scalable. The data center standard.

quiz.question: How many network hops does it take for any two servers in a spine-leaf fabric?

details.summary: Spine-leaf architecture uses two layers of switches where every leaf switch connects to every spine switch, creating a fabric with predictable latency and equal bandwidth between any two servers.
details.whyItMatters: Modern applications generate massive server-to-server traffic. Spine-leaf architecture provides consistent performance for this east-west traffic, which traditional hierarchical designs cannot match.
takeaways: Every leaf connects to every spine for equal-cost paths
Latency is predictable: always exactly two hops between any servers
Scales horizontally by adding more spine or leaf switches

faq.question: How does spine-leaf differ from a three-tier network?
faq.answer: Three-tier networks use core, distribution, and access layers with potential bottlenecks at higher tiers. Spine-leaf uses just two layers where every leaf connects to every spine, ensuring consistent one-hop latency between any two leaf switches. It scales better for server-to-server traffic.

faq.question: When should you use spine-leaf architecture?
faq.answer: Spine-leaf is ideal for data centers with significant east-west traffic between servers, which includes most modern application architectures. Small networks under 100 servers may not need this complexity. Campus networks typically still use traditional hierarchical designs.
